fixes.explanation: False is right, friend. The text says, “He pursues them, going on safely, hardly touching the path with his feet.” (Isaiah 41:3). He's the one doing the chasing, and nothing there says he's dragging or struggling. Feet that hardly touch the path and a man going on safely sound like someone moving with ease.

Not the kings of the islands, baker. The question is who performed this and carried it out, calling forth the generations from the beginning. The LORD answers it Himself with “…I am He.” (Isaiah 41:4). Nobody else gets named as the answer.
Fear, baker. The text says, “The islands see and fear; the ends of the earth tremble.” (Isaiah 41:5). The islands see, and fear is what comes next. They also approach and come forward.

Scattering makes sense if you're scared, baker. But the text says, “They approach and come forward.” (Isaiah 41:5). They fear and the ends of the earth tremble, and still they approach. I'd have scattered at the first sign of trouble.

Be strong, baker. “Each one helps the other and says to his brother, ‘Be strong!’” (Isaiah 41:6). It's people lifting each other up while the ends of the earth tremble. Everybody needs a friend like that in the moment.

Nail it down, baker. “He nails it down so it will not be toppled.” (Isaiah 41:7). Just before that, the one who wields the hammer cheers on the one who strikes the anvil, saying of the welding, “It is good.” When I really want my cookie boxes to stay shut, I'm not shy with the tape either.
A hill is a fine spot, baker, but the text never puts it there. The verse says, “He nails it down so it will not be toppled.” (Isaiah 41:7). A nail is what keeps it from toppling.

Firstborn sounds official, friend, but it isn't what the LORD says here. He says, “…descendant of Abraham My friend—” (Isaiah 41:8). Firstborn is nowhere in the verse, but “friend” is right there. Of all the things He could call Abraham, that's the word He picks.

Shepherd has a nice ring to it, baker, but it's not the word for Abraham here. The LORD says, “…descendant of Abraham My friend—” (Isaiah 41:8). The title is “friend,” plain and warm. I'd happily take that one from the LORD myself.

Strengthen, baker. “I will strengthen you; I will surely help you; I will uphold you with My righteous right hand.” (Isaiah 41:10). Strength, help and upholding all come in one breath. Hard to ask for a better promise.

The Holy One of Israel, baker. The LORD says, “Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel.” (Isaiah 41:14). Right before that He says, “Do not fear, O Jacob, you worm, O few men of Israel.” Then He names who stands behind them, and that name is worth remembering.

That's an easy thing to do after a win, friend, but it's not what the text says. “But you will rejoice in the LORD; you will glory in the Holy One of Israel.” (Isaiah 41:16). That comes right after the wind carries the chaff away. Their glory is in Him, not in themselves.

Mourning over the mountains isn't in the text, baker. “But you will rejoice in the LORD; you will glory in the Holy One of Israel.” (Isaiah 41:16). That comes right after the wind carries the chaff away and a gale scatters it. The response the text gives is rejoicing.

This one is true, friend. The LORD says of the poor and needy, “I, the LORD, will answer them; I, the God of Israel, will not forsake them.” (Isaiah 41:17). Their tongues are parched with thirst, and He says He will answer them. So True is the one that matches the text.

Desert, baker. “I will turn the desert into a pool of water, and the dry land into flowing springs.” (Isaiah 41:18). A desert becomes a pool of water. The dry land gets flowing springs too, and that's quite a change.

City isn't in that verse, baker. The LORD says, “I will turn the desert into a pool of water, and the dry land into flowing springs.” (Isaiah 41:18). The desert is what becomes the pool. The dry land becomes the springs.
